title: Three agents, one search
scenario: A consulting team built a research assistant: a lead agent that starts subagents in parallel. Its first real report missed half the question. You also get two smaller questions from other teams (exhibit).
exhibit:
QUESTION: How did the chip shortage hit car makers in 2021,
          and how do supply chains look in 2025?

LEAD AGENT -> subagent prompts
  sub 1: "research the semiconductor shortage"
  sub 2: "research the semiconductor shortage"
  sub 3: "look into chips"

RESULTS
  sub 1: 2025 supply chains
  sub 2: 2025 supply chains (same sources as sub 1)
  sub 3: general history of chip making
  nobody: 2021 car production cuts

OTHER TEAMS
  A) Support bot, OpenAI Agents SDK: a triage agent and a billing
     specialist. Once a ticket is about billing, the specialist
     must answer the customer directly.
  B) A developer wants 5 parallel subagents to fix one typo
     in one file.

questions.prompt: Why did two subagents repeat the same work while 2021 went uncovered?

options.text: Subagents share one context window, so they read each other's searches.
options.explanation: The opposite: each subagent has its own context. That is why they could not see they were duplicating.

options.text: Three subagents is too many for a two-part question.
options.explanation: Two parts with two time periods fits a few subagents well. The problem is what each one was told.

options.text: The delegation prompts were vague, with no objective or boundaries.
options.explanation: Right. Anthropic saw the same thing: short tasks like research the semiconductor shortage made subagents misread the task or repeat each other's searches.

options.text: The subagents ran on a weaker model than the lead agent.
options.explanation: Nothing in the exhibit shows the models. Even a strong model can't guess a split of work it was never given.

questions.prompt: Which new prompt for sub 1 follows Anthropic's delegation advice?

options.text: "Research the semiconductor shortage in depth. Be thorough."
options.explanation: Still no boundary or output format, so it can overlap with the others again.

options.text: "Research everything about chips; the lead agent will filter it."
options.explanation: That spends the most tokens and pushes all the filtering back into the lead's context.

options.text: "Read the full lead conversation first, then decide what to do."
options.explanation: It gets no parent conversation, only the prompt you pass (plus its own system prompt and CLAUDE.md).

options.text: "2021 car production cuts only; not 2025. News and company reports. Bullet list with a URL per line."
options.explanation: Right. It has an objective, a clear boundary, guidance on sources and an output format.

questions.prompt: Team A: the billing specialist must answer the customer directly. Which OpenAI pattern fits?

options.text: A handoff from the triage agent to the billing specialist.
options.explanation: Right. In a handoff, control moves to the specialist, which owns the next response.

options.text: The billing specialist as a tool of the triage agent, via `as_tool()`.
options.explanation: With agents as tools, the manager keeps ownership of the reply. Here the specialist must answer directly.

options.text: One agent with the billing instructions pasted into its prompt.
options.explanation: That can work for small cases, but the team wants a separate specialist that owns billing replies.

options.text: Run both agents in parallel and show the faster answer.
options.explanation: That doubles the cost and gives no clear owner of the reply, which OpenAI says is the first design choice.

questions.prompt: Team B wants 5 parallel subagents for one typo in one file. What is your advice?

options.text: Yes: parallel subagents always finish faster than one agent.
options.explanation: Parallel work only helps when there are independent subtasks. One typo has none.

options.text: Use one agent. Subagents add tokens and there is nothing to split.
options.explanation: Right. Multi-agent systems used about 15× the tokens of chat in Anthropic's data, and OpenAI says to start with one agent whenever you can.

options.text: Use 5 subagents, but give each one only Read and Grep.
options.explanation: Then none of them can fix the typo, and the cost is still five agents.

options.text: Use a handoff chain of 5 agents, one per line of the file.
options.explanation: That adds prompts, traces and approval surfaces with no benefit, which OpenAI warns about.
